_readme: P1 authored optional scenes (decided 2026-10-02; implemented 2026-10-04). Each month the scene router picks at most one optional scene from every system's eligible candidates (commissions, invitations, Grand Challenges, people's lives and these), keeping any category from a third scene in a row while something else could happen (SYSTEMS §2, scene pacing). A scene here happens once, when all its 'requires' hold (people.json syntax plus month:<1-12>, monthsIn:<n>, machine:assessed, machine:steps:<n>, project:<id>:done, knows:<person>, scene:<id>, flag:<name>; '!x' for not, 'a|b' for either). Reusable texture: 'cooldownMonths' and 'variants' (each variant's text used once, never the same words twice). Effects: 'gold' (aurei at AD 155 prices), 'triggers' (a choice from events.json), 'regard' (a person's regard for you) and 'status' (a person's standing line). Roman life is woven into routine and tied to the people and work of the game, never free-floating filler. The machine mystery keeps the R-17 thread alive and is not explained early. Weights default to scenes.baseWeight.

scenes.text: At the small baths behind the Circus Maximus you sit in the warm room between a fuller and a man selling olives. The olive man complains that a merchant under the Aventine pays porters to bail his cellar every morning, and still the jars go green. The fuller says the merchant should sacrifice to the river and stop complaining.

Felix has you to dinner on the Kalends. Before anyone eats, his boys put a pinch of meal and a drop of wine before the little shrine by the door, where two dancing Lares stand on either side of a painted snake. Prima asks where your household gods are. Felix answers for you: in a box, travelling. Everyone laughs, and Prima keeps looking at you.

A rope-maker of the guild has died. The members walk behind the bier to the tombs on the Ostia road, with flute players and a woman paid to wail. The guild pays for the burial out of the box you saw passed round at supper. Felix walks beside you and names the men as they pass: who owes whom, who will want the dead man's yard.

Saturnalia. Cassianus wears a felt cap like a freed slave and serves his own porters at table, badly, while his sister keeps an eye on the good cups. A porter is king of the feast and orders Cassianus to sing. He sings. He gives you a wax candle and a clay figure of a dog, and expects nothing so grand in return.

Felix drags you to the Circus Maximus to watch the Blues. Two hundred thousand people, the smell of roasting chickpeas, men laying bets, a baker scratching a curse against the Green driver onto a strip of lead. The Blue chariot clips the turning post on the fourth lap and the Greens take it. Felix does not speak to you until you are back across the river.

status.Cassianus: suing Pollio before the praetor over the pump

scenes.text: In the Forum, under an awning, Cassianus's advocate argues before the praetor's man that Pollio's pump slanders his client's goods. Pollio's advocate says nobody owns the shape of a pump. Both name you. The case is put off until after the games, as most cases are.

Prima has made a vow at the sanctuary of Aesculapius on the Tiber Island: a clay leg, because the fever settled in Felix's knee, and a cockerel if he walks to the quays by the Ides. You carry broth to their room and find two physicians arguing over him. He walks to the quays on the twelfth. Prima buys the cockerel.

Diodoros asks you to come with him to a letter-writer in the Forum, a Greek with ink on his fingers who charges by the line. Diodoros dictates to his mother in Antioch: the hand is healing, the work is better, he is not gambling. The letter-writer looks at you over the last line and writes it anyway.

The smith takes you to the tavern by the Porta Trigemina after the forge is banked. Dice, cheap wine cut with sea water, a painted Mercury on the wall with a purse in his hand. A veteran of the German wars wins every throw and shows everyone the scar that pays his pension.

A physician called Serenus finds you at the fountain, a short man with ink on his cuffs. He has heard you talk about fevers as if you'd counted them. "Have you?" he asks. You say not yet. "Neither has anyone else," he says. "Come and see my casebooks. Bring wine; my sister won't buy any."

Serenus spreads two years of fever cases across his sister's table: the purge, the bleeding, the cold baths, who lived. You show him how to rule the wax into columns, one case to a line, the same questions for every patient. He tries it on the last month's cases and goes quiet. "The bleeding," he says. "I bled eleven of them."

The bronzesmith from the Clivus who argued longest over your foot comes to find you. Gaius Fabius Crispus, he says, as if you should know it. "I cut twenty seats to your bar this month and every one fitted. I don't like being told how to cut. I like losing work less." He wants to know what else you can measure.

Gaius has you to dinner above the shop: lentils, sausage, a jug of Sabine wine. His wife Livia has a green ribbon in her hair for the races and asks whether foreigners are allowed to have opinions about chariots. When you say the Blues looked strong she tells Gaius to stop inviting you. She refills your cup anyway.

Gaius's nephew Marcus is at the bench, filing a bearing shell that is already round. He tells you he could run the shop better than his uncle. Then he asks what the marks on your wax tablet mean, and when you tell him he says he knew that already.

You find Marcus scratching a tally on the shop wall: every time the shaft stops, a mark, and the reason beside it in letters that slope downhill. Nobody asked him to. You show him how to keep it in a wax book instead, one line a day. He says a man who writes things down is a clerk. The next morning the book is full.

Gaius takes you up the Janiculum to the mills, where the water of the Aqua Traiana comes down in a race and turns wheel after wheel. The millwright, Aulus Septimius Crispus, is up to his knees in the tail race clearing mud. He looks at your drawing of one wheel driving four machines. "Where does a man stand to grease that one?" he says, and goes back to the mud.

Old Lucan, who taught Gaius, watches you explain the shaft at the tavern with a finger in spilled wine. When you finish he turns your cup upside down. "Do not become a man who only has ideas," he says. "Come to my forge tomorrow. I'll show you why your cutters will break." They break exactly where he said.

Livia has had a son. On the ninth day Gaius closes the shop for the naming: the household gods garlanded, a sow sacrificed, the boy given a bulla to wear against the evil eye and the name Lucius. The shaft can wait, Gaius says, and when you look at the race he says it again, more slowly.

A finishing-shop owner, Sextus Nerius, comes to watch the grinder. Twelve men polish and fit bronze in his shop by hand, some of them for twenty years. He watches the wheel take the rough off a casting in the time it takes one of his men to find his file. He doesn't say anything. He comes back the next day and watches again.

Up at the mills before dawn, you hear the wheel start, and at the same moment, back at the workshop, the machine's panel wakes on its own. The log shows a short burst of signal and an answer: the same pattern as the last second before the crash, a request and an acceptance. Nothing in Rome is sending anything.

Someone has nailed a curse tablet to the bath-house door, a strip of lead folded twice. Philippus reads it out in the warm room for the laughs: may his water run cold, may his furnace smoke, may the foreigner who fixed his pipe lose his teeth. The fuller downstream says he can't read. Nobody believes him.

A notice is painted on the wall at the end of the street: by order of the curator of waters, all private taps on the Circus branch will be inspected. Two of the curator's slaves walk the pipe with a ladder. By the end of the week the fuller's tap is cut, his vats stand empty, and four of his men are looking for work. Philippus's hot room has never been hotter.

Serenus reads Pomponia's tablets to the Circle and says the fever came from bad air rising off the cistern. You say it was the water. He says water is water, and air is where fever lives, and Hippocrates agrees with him. You argue until his sister throws you both out. The next week he sends you a jar of honey and the tablets from another household, with the cisterns marked.

Cassianus comes to you with the marriage contract, a wax tablet in a wooden case. Seven witnesses must seal it. He has six: his sister's husband, two shippers, a neighbor, the grain factor's brother, his own accountant. "You are respectable now," he says, not quite a question.

Felix comes to the workshop after dark and talks about the weather, the Blues and a shipment of cordage for ten minutes before he gets to it. The rhetor wants another term's fees, and the moneylender in the Velabrum wants a third of it back again by the Ides.

You go to Diodoros's funeral meal for his mother: bread, lentils, a jug of wine, a dozen porters in a cookshop by the river. Someone has drawn a little face on the wall above the table and written her name in Greek letters. The porters toast her nine times and Diodoros tells stories about Antioch that may not be true.

Serenus asks you to stand at the back of the hall while he reads his fevers to anyone who will come. Eleven people come, three of them physicians, one of them asleep. He reads every case. Afterward a young woman from the Subura asks him to come and see her children, and he goes.

Livia takes you to the Circus for the September games and makes you wear a green ribbon. The Greens win the first race and she throws a whole bag of sunflower seeds over the heads of the Blues in the row below. Gaius, beside her, keeps his hands in his lap and smiles at nothing.

Marcus files a shell down too far and blames the gauge. You show him the gauge is right. He throws the file across the shop and says his father was a clerk and he will not be talked to like one. Gaius sends him home. The shell goes in the scrap bin and nobody mentions it for a week.

You show Aulus a drawing with a gear train to change the speed of the grinder. He looks at it for a long time. "Mud," he says. "Every one of those teeth fills with mud in March, and the man who cleans them loses a finger in April. Use a bigger pulley." You use a bigger pulley.

The smiths walk Lucan's ashes out the Porta Ostiensis to the burial club's tomb, a little house of brick with niches like a dovecote. Each man drops a nail into the urn's niche before it is closed. His granddaughter sells eggs to the mourners afterward; Lucan would have approved.

You pass Sextus Nerius's shop on the Clivus. Through the door you can hear the grinder and, under it, men talking as they work. One of the old finishers is teaching a boy to judge a polish by the way it holds the light. Sextus sees you and nods, and doesn't come out.

Market day at the Forum Holitorium. You buy bread, a cheese wrapped in leaves, and a bunch of leeks, and you pay too much for all of it. The cheese woman knows you are foreign by the way you count, and charges for it.
variants: At the market a sausage seller shouts that his sausages are from Lucania and his prices are from heaven. A man with a basket of snails haggles with him over a trade and wins. You eat a sausage standing up, the Roman way, and burn your mouth.

The price of wheat is chalked on a board by the grain sellers' stalls, and the women around it argue about the number as if it were a person. A girl sells you figs and gives you the change in a coin so worn you can't tell whose head is on it.

Market day, and it is raining. The stallholders pull hides over their goods and keep shouting. You buy lamp oil from a man who swears it is Spanish and smells of fish. Under the awning of a wine shop two old men are playing knucklebones for olives.

A crowd at the market around a man selling a cure for everything from a painted cart: fevers, gout, sorrow, failing hair. Three people buy. You think of Serenus's columns and almost laugh, and the man sees you and offers you a discount.
The fishmongers by the river have a sturgeon as long as a man laid out on a slab. A cook from a senator's house buys it whole, and four porters carry it up the Caelian like a funeral.

A market inspector, an aedile's man, walks the stalls with a set of bronze weights, checking the bakers' scales. One baker is found short and fined on the spot. The crowd enjoys it more than the theater.

Market day, and a slave dealer has set up at the edge of the Forum with a dozen people on a platform, each with a placard round the neck listing age, origin and faults. Customers walk past it to buy cabbages.

scenes.text: At the district fountain the women wait their turn with jars on their hips and trade news faster than any messenger: a midwife who drinks, a baby born with a caul, the price of leeks, a husband seen somewhere he shouldn't have been. They stop talking when you come near and start again when you leave.
variants: The fountain runs clean and cold, and the boys of the street have found out that a thumb over the spout soaks anyone passing. You are passing. An old woman laughs so hard she has to put her jar down.

A water-carrier with two jars on a yoke tells you he used to walk to the Aqua Marcia for clean water. Now he sells to the top floors of the insulae, where nobody wants to carry anything up six flights, and makes a better living than before.
At the fountain the talk is of a neighbor's son who has joined the vigiles: good pay, a bed, a uniform, and every fire in the city to run into.
The women at the fountain have heard about you. One asks if it's true you can fix anything. Another asks if you're married. A third asks both at once, and they all laugh.

scenes.text: At the broken fountain the women queue at a trickle and argue about whose turn it is. One of them has walked from three streets over. A girl falls asleep against the basin waiting.
variants: The broken fountain has a pool of green water around its base now, and boys float bark boats in it. A woman pulls her son out by the ear and tells him that's where fevers come from. She may be right.

scenes.text: A night in the tavern on the corner: a jug of rough red, a plate of chickpeas, and a dice game you are talked into and lose. The landlord has painted on the wall what a cup costs, so nobody can argue. People argue anyway.
variants: In the tavern a sailor from Alexandria tells everyone the lighthouse there is twice the height of anything in Rome. A man from the Subura offers to fight him over it. The landlord stops them by putting a free jug on the table, and charges for it later.
Someone has scratched on the tavern wall, beside the price list, a long complaint that the landlord waters his wine and pisses in the jugs. Underneath, in a different hand: and you drank it.

In the tavern a veteran with one ear sings a marching song about a general's bald head. The whole room knows the chorus. The landlord's wife throws him out at the third verse, and he comes back in for the fourth.
A quiet night in the tavern. A scribe is writing a letter for a soldier's mother, reading each line back aloud. By the end half the tavern is helping with the wording.

scenes.text: Before dawn you go with Cassianus to his patron's house on the Caelian, where twenty men in togas wait in the street to say good morning to a senator's freedman, who says good morning to the senator. Cassianus gets a nod and a small basket of food. On the way back he says it was a good morning, and means it.

Under an awning at the edge of the Forum a schoolmaster drills a dozen boys in their letters: they chant the alphabet forwards, backwards, and in pairs, and the slowest gets the cane across his palm. A slave boy sits at the back holding his young master's tablets and learns faster than any of them.

At the Ludi Apollinares you go to the theater of Marcellus to see an old comedy: a clever slave, two foolish fathers, a lost daughter found. The audience knows every joke before it comes and laughs harder for it. Afterward a mime does a drunk senator and nobody laughs at all, and the mime is very pleased.
variants: The games again, a tragedy this time: Medea, in Latin, very loud. A woman behind you weeps for the children every time and eats almonds between the weeping.
At the games a troupe of pantomime dancers plays the loves of Mars and Venus without a word spoken, only a chorus and pipes. The crowd knows the dancer by name and chants it until he comes out again.

scenes.text: A fire in an insula behind the Circus at night. The vigiles come with buckets, axes and a pump on a cart, and the street makes a chain from the nearest fountain. They pull down the next house to stop it spreading. By dawn two families are sitting on their furniture in the street, and the pump's leather flaps are hanging in strips.

High summer. Anyone with money has gone to the hills. The streets stink by noon, the fountains run warm, and the physicians say the bad air rises off the Tiber marshes at dusk. You keep the shutters closed and work at night.
variants: Another summer of heat. Felix sends his boys to an uncle at Tibur. The baths are full from dawn and the bath-keepers raise their prices, and nobody can stop them.

Summer, and a dry one: the Tiber is low enough to show the old piers, and boys dive for coins off them. The grain barges scrape bottom coming up from Ostia and the price of bread goes up a little, as it does.

scenes.text: Winter fog on the river. Everyone in the insula cooks on a brazier, and the stairwell smells of charcoal and fish sauce. A man two floors down has died of the fumes, which happens every winter, and the landlord says it happens every winter.
variants: A cold January: the fountains freeze at the edges, the bathhouses can't keep the hot room hot, and the price of charcoal doubles. Gaius sleeps at the shop to keep the furnace in.
Winter again. The streets are quiet after dark; the lamplighters don't bother with the alleys. You go home by the main streets with a hand on your knife, the way everyone does.

scenes.text: At the Porticus Minucia the citizens queue for their monthly grain with bronze tokens in their hands. Diodoros, who isn't a citizen, watches from across the street. "Your city feeds its own," he says. "The rest of us buy bread." A clerk checks each token against a list as long as the portico.

Lupercalia: young men of good family run half naked round the Palatine with strips of goatskin, striking anyone in reach. Young wives step out to be struck, for luck with children. Livia's sister does; Livia doesn't, and says loudly why not.
variants: Lupercalia again. This year a running boy catches a magistrate's wife across the face with the goatskin and the whole street holds its breath until she laughs.
At Lupercalia the runners are thinner this year and the crowd smaller. An old man tells you that in his father's day the senators ran too, and nobody believes him.

scenes.text: For the Parentalia Livia takes bread soaked in wine and a few violets out to her parents' tomb on the Via Appia, and you carry the basket. She pours the wine through a pipe into the ground so they can drink it. On the way back she is quieter than you have ever heard her, and then she isn't.
variants: Parentalia again. Livia takes the girls this time and teaches them what to pour and where. The younger one asks if her grandparents can taste the wine. Livia says yes, and drinks a little herself to make sure.

For Parentalia the whole Via Appia smells of violets and wine. Families picnic by their tombs. Gaius's mother's niche has a new crack, and he spends the afternoon arguing with the tomb's keeper about who will pay to mend it.

scenes.text: Saturnalia at Gaius's: the shop shut, the old slave who keeps the furnace sitting at the head of the table and giving orders, Marcus made to serve the wine. Livia gives you a little clay lamp with a gladiator on it. Gaius gives you a file he made himself, which from Gaius is a speech.

Pomponia asks you to dinner. You recline on the lowest couch, beside Serenus, who eats with concentration while a freedman reads Greek poetry nobody listens to. Pomponia asks your opinion of her new cistern lid in front of everyone. A senator's wife at the top couch asks who you are, and nobody quite knows.

Successus's apprentice has run off to join a troupe of acrobats going to Capua. Successus says good riddance and spends the whole day looking out of the door. The boy's mother comes to apologize and leaves a cheese.

The legions are back from the East. Veterans fill the taverns with tales of Ctesiphon and Seleucia, show off silk and scars, and pay for everything in eastern coin. Some of them are coughing. Nobody minds yet.

On the Via Appia, among the great tombs, a small one has a carved relief of a baker at his oven and an inscription longer than the tomb is wide: once a slave, now free, a baker, he built this for himself, his wife and his freedmen, and wishes the reader good health. A boy is relieving himself against the next tomb along.
Prima hears you may be going on a long journey and sends you to the temple of Fortuna Redux by the Porta Capena. "Make a vow," she says. "People who come back make vows. People who don't, didn't."

Your neighbors in the insula: a cobbler on the ground floor who sings, a family of six on your landing who share one brazier, and a widow above who drops her slops into the street with a shout of warning that comes a moment too late.
variants: The landlord's agent comes for the rent and finds the family on your landing a month behind. He threatens, they plead, the cobbler downstairs lends them half. By evening everyone is sitting on the stairs together eating his bread.

A baby is born on your landing in the night. In the morning the father hangs a garland on the door and puts a little altar to Juno on the step. The widow upstairs comes down for the first time in a month to look.
The insula's water comes from a fountain at the end of the street, and the stairs are steep. A boy from the top floor charges an as a jar to carry it up. He is saving to buy a dog.
A crack runs down the wall of your room after a heavy cart passes in the night. The landlord says the building has stood forty years. The cobbler downstairs says that is exactly the trouble.
The cobbler's wife has left him for a sausage maker from the next street. The cobbler sings sadder songs and makes better shoes.

scenes.text: An afternoon at the baths: exercise in the courtyard, the hot room, the warm room, the cold plunge, then oil and a strigil. The real business is talk. You hear about three lawsuits, two scandals and a ship lost off Sicily before you are dry.
variants: At the baths a man selling cakes walks round the pool shouting, a hair-plucker's customers shriek, and a ball game in the courtyard sends a ball into the hot room. Nobody seems to find any of it strange but you.
In the steam a senator's freedman tells anyone who listens how much his master's new villa cost. A builder in the corner says quietly that it cost half that, and he should know.

The baths are crowded with soldiers on leave. They oil each other, wrestle, and argue about pay. One of them tells you the army's coins are getting lighter every year and the officers pretend not to notice.
At the baths you see Felix, Cassianus's sister and the cheese woman from the market, all in one afternoon. Rome is a million people and you keep meeting the same twenty.

scenes.text: A sacrifice at the temple of Castor in the Forum: a white heifer garlanded, the priest's head covered, a flute playing so nobody hears an unlucky word. The haruspex reads the liver and pronounces it favorable. The meat is sold afterward at a stall by the steps.
variants: At the temple of Ceres the plebeian aediles hand out bread to the poor on the goddess's day. The line goes around the Aventine. Diodoros, who isn't entitled to any, gets two loaves anyway, from a woman who likes his face.

A procession for Magna Mater: her eunuch priests in bright robes, cymbals, tambourines, men cutting their own arms until they bleed. The crowd parts for them, half afraid, half delighted. Livia covers the girls' eyes and watches herself.

scenes.text: In the Basilica Julia four courts sit at once, separated by curtains, and the advocates' voices carry over all of them. You watch a case about a stolen mule. The mule is brought in as evidence. It does not testify.
variants: A day in the courts: a will contested by three nephews, each with his own advocate and his own claque of paid applauders. The judge falls asleep. The applauders don't.

In the Forum a man has a contract witnessed: seven witnesses, seven seals, an argument over whether the fourth witness is really a citizen. You think of how many of Rome's agreements depend on someone's ring.

scenes.text: The old emperor is dead at his villa at Lorium, and his body comes into the city on a bier carried by magistrates. The shops close. Two men are emperors now, Marcus and his brother Lucius, and the coins with both their heads are in the market within the month.

Recruiters are in the Forum: the war with Parthia needs men. A centurion with a vine stick looks over the young men who come forward, checks their teeth like a horse dealer's, and turns away half. A boy from your insula is taken; his mother walks beside him as far as the Porta Capena.
A courier from the East rides in through the Porta Flaminia, and by evening the whole city knows: Armenia retaken. The baths are full of men who have never been east of Ostia explaining the campaign.
variants: News from the East: the legions have crossed the Euphrates. A sausage seller has renamed his best sausage after the general. It is the same sausage.
More news from the East: Ctesiphon taken and burned. There are games for it, three days of them, and the price of grain goes up again because the ships are carrying soldiers.

scenes.text: The grain ships are late from Alexandria and the bakers' loaves get smaller without getting cheaper. At the fountain the women say the emperor will fix it. At the tavern the men say the bakers are hoarding.
variants: Bread is short again. A crowd gathers at the bakers' street and someone throws a stone through a shutter. The urban cohorts come and stand about with their shields, and the bread comes, eventually.
The grain fleet comes in all at once after a month of nothing: two hundred ships in the harbor at Ostia, and every barge on the river busy. Lollius's men work three days without sleeping.

scenes.text: Compitalia: at the shrine where four streets cross, the neighborhood hangs a woolen doll for every free person and a woolen ball for every slave, for the Lares of the crossroads to take instead of them. The street magistrate, a freedman in a borrowed toga, pours the wine. Your insula hangs a doll for you without asking.
variants: Compitalia again. The crossroads shrine has a new coat of paint: two Lares dancing, a snake, a pig being led to sacrifice. The painter is the cobbler's nephew and has given one Lar the cobbler's face.
At the crossroads shrine this Compitalia the street magistrate is a baker you buy from. He makes a speech about the neighborhood that goes on too long and ends with free bread, so nobody minds.
Compitalia, and the dolls on the crossroads shrine are fewer this year. The street magistrate reads the names of neighbors who died in the year before he pours the wine.

scenes.text: The Ludi Romani: a procession from the Capitol to the Circus, the gods carried on litters, dancers, boxers, men dressed as satyrs mocking the dancers. Then the races. The crowd is a single animal, and for an afternoon you are part of it.
variants: The Ludi Romani again, and gladiators this year in the Flavian amphitheater as well as the races. The crowd boos a fighter who won't finish a fallen man and cheers when the editor spares him. You leave before the beasts.

At this year's Ludi Romani it rains on the procession. The gods' litters are covered with oiled cloth and the dancers dance anyway. The races run in mud; a Red driver wins for the first time in years and his supporters riot happily.

scenes.text: Painted on the wall of a fuller's yard in red letters a yard high: a show of gladiators, twenty pairs, awnings provided. Below it, smaller, in charcoal: Successus loves Iris, and Iris doesn't care.
variants: On a shop wall someone has painted a notice for a lost donkey, a reward, and a description so detailed you could pick the donkey out in a crowd. Underneath, another hand: found it, ate it.
A new notice on the street corner: apartments to let in the insula of Arrius, shops with lodgings above, first floor for gentlemen. In smaller letters: no dyers.
Someone has scratched a long list of debts on the tavern wall, with names. By the end of the week half the names are scratched out and the list has a new heading: paid, or dead.

scenes.text: Cleaning the navigation panel, you wake the event log. The last entries before the crash scroll past: a stability check, a field warm-up you never started, and then two lines you didn't write. REQUEST. REFERENCE REQUEST ACCEPTED — R-17. Four seconds later, the destination locks: 155-03-ROMA. The timestamp is a second before you threw the switch.

With the coil housing sealed, the panel stays lit for a full night. Near dawn it prints, unprompted, LINK QUALITY: DEGRADED, and a little bar half filled. Nothing in Rome is linked to anything. You sit with the panel until the light goes out.

You run a reference test, the kind you ran a hundred times in the lab. The answer comes back faster than the machine could compute it: REMOTE REFERENCE ACKNOWLEDGED. You run it again with a wrong value on purpose. It acknowledges that too, and corrects it.

The last repair holds. Every light on the panel comes up together, and one you have never seen lit: R-17 ACTIVE. You go back through the crash log line by line. The destination was set before the field came up. The machine didn't pick Rome when it failed. It had already been told where to go.

You leave the channel open. Every few nights, at no hour you can predict, the panel wakes and prints the same three lines, REQUEST RECEIVED, SOURCE: R-17, DO NOT JUMP, and goes dark. You start keeping the times on a wax tablet. The gaps between them are not random, and they are not anything you recognize.

The panel stays dark under its sacking. Some nights you lie awake listening for it anyway. Once you lift the cloth and the indicator under it, the one you never saw lit before the crash, is glowing faintly on its own.

In the bottom of your pack, under the spare gloves, is your old lab notebook. Most of it is load tables. On a page from the month before the crash, in your own hand, is a citation you don't remember writing down: R17, a paper on temporal-reference stability, and underlined twice, the words 'reciprocal lock'. Nothing else on the page. You read it until the lamp runs out.
